title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXV
paragraphs:
“Love seeketh not itself to please,
Nor for itself hath any care
But for another gives its ease
And builds a heaven in hell’s despair.
. . . . . . .
Love seeketh only self to please,
To bind another to its delight,
Joys in another’s loss of ease,
And builds a hell in heaven’s despite.”
—W. BLAKE: _Songs of Experience_.

Fred wanted to reach Stone Court when Mary would not expect him and his uncle was still upstairs. Then she might be alone in the paneled parlor. He left his horse in the yard to avoid sounding on the gravel in front and entered without warning beyond the turn of the door handle. Mary sat in her usual corner, laughing over Mrs. Piozzi's memories of Johnson. The amusement was still on her face as she looked up. It gradually faded when Fred approached without a word and stood before her, looking ill, his elbow on the mantelpiece. She remained silent too, merely raising her eyes in a question.
“Mary,” he began, “I'm a worthless scoundrel.”
“One of those descriptions at a time should be enough,” she said, attempting a smile but feeling alarmed.
“I know you'll never think well of me again. You'll think I'm a liar, dishonest, that I didn't care for you or your parents. You always think the worst of me anyway.”
“I can't deny I'll think all that if you give me good reasons, Fred. But please tell me immediately what you've done. I'd rather hear the painful truth than imagine it.”

“I owed a hundred and sixty pounds. I asked your father to sign a bill as security. I thought it wouldn't affect him. I was certain I'd pay it myself, and I've tried as hard as I could. But I've been so unlucky. A horse turned out badly, and I can only pay fifty pounds. I can't ask my father; he wouldn't give me a penny. My uncle gave me a hundred not long ago. What can I do? Your father has no money to spare, so your mother will have to use the ninety-two pounds she's saved. She says your savings must go too. You see what a—”

“Oh, poor mother! Poor father!” Mary's eyes filled, and a small sob rose which she tried to suppress. She stared ahead without attending to Fred as all the consequences at home came before her. He too was silent for a while, more miserable than ever. Finally he said, “I wouldn't have hurt you for anything, Mary. You'll never forgive me.”

“What difference does my forgiveness make?” Mary asked passionately. “Would it make things easier for mother to lose the money she's earned by teaching for four years so she could send Alfred to Mr. Hanmer? Would you find all that pleasant enough if I forgave you?”
“Say anything you want. I deserve it.”
“I don't want to say anything,” Mary replied more quietly. “My anger won't help.” She wiped her eyes, put aside the book, and went to fetch her sewing.
Fred watched her, hoping she would meet his eyes and give his pleading remorse a way in. But no; she could easily avoid looking up.

“I do care about your mother losing her money,” he said once she was seated and sewing quickly. “I wanted to ask, Mary—don't you think Mr. Featherstone might advance the money if you told him? About Alfred's apprenticeship, I mean.”

“My family doesn't like begging, Fred. We'd rather earn our money. Besides, you say Mr. Featherstone recently gave you a hundred pounds. He seldom gives presents, and has never given any to us. Father certainly won't ask him for anything. Even if I wanted to beg, it would do no good.”
“I'm so miserable, Mary. If you knew how miserable, you'd pity me.”
“There are things more deserving of pity. But selfish people always consider their own discomfort more important than anything in the world. I see enough of that every day.”
“It's hardly fair to call me selfish. If you knew what other young men do, you'd think me far from the worst.”
“I know that people who spend a great deal on themselves without knowing how they'll pay must be selfish. They're always thinking about what they can get, never what others may lose.”
“Anyone can have bad luck and be unable to pay despite intending to, Mary. There's no better man than your father, yet he got into difficulties.”

“How dare you compare yourself with my father?” Mary asked in a deep voice of indignation. “He didn't get into trouble by thinking about idle pleasures. He was always thinking about work for other people. And he lived hard and worked hard to repay everyone's loss.”

“And you think I'll never try to make anything good. It's ungenerous to believe the worst of a man. When you have influence over him, you might try using it to improve him, but you never do. Anyway, I'm leaving,” Fred finished wearily. “I'll never speak to you about anything again. I'm very sorry for all the trouble I've caused. That's all.”

Mary let her sewing fall and looked up. Even a girl's love often contains something motherly, and Mary's hard experience had made her sensitive in a way very different from the brittle, shallow thing we call girlishness. Fred's final words sent a sudden pang through her, like a mother's at imagining the cries of her naughty, wandering child who might get lost and hurt. When she met his dull, hopeless gaze, pity overcame her anger and every other anxiety.

“Oh, Fred, you look so ill! Sit down a moment. Don't leave yet. Let me tell uncle you're here. He's been wondering why he hasn't seen you all week.” She spoke quickly, saying whatever came first without quite knowing the words, her voice half soothing, half pleading. She rose as if to fetch Mr. Featherstone. Naturally Fred felt as if the clouds had parted to let in light. He moved into her path.
“Say one word, Mary, and I'll do anything. Say you won't think the worst of me, won't give me up completely.”

“As though thinking badly of you gave me pleasure,” Mary said sadly. “As though seeing you idle and frivolous didn't hurt. How can you bear to be so contemptible while others work and struggle and so much needs doing? How can you bear to be useful for nothing? And with so much goodness in your nature, Fred. You could be worth a great deal.”
“I'll try to become anything you want, if you'll tell me you love me.”

“I'd be ashamed to say I loved a man who was always depending on others and counting on what they'd do for him. What will you be at forty? Like Mr. Bowyer, I suppose: just as idle, living in Mrs. Beck's front parlor, fat and shabby, hoping someone invites you to dinner, spending the morning learning a comic song. Oh no, learning a tune on the flute.”

Her lips had begun to curve into a smile as soon as she asked about his future—young spirits change quickly—and by the end her face shone with amusement. Her ability to laugh at him relieved Fred like the ending of pain. With a yielding little smile he tried to take her hand. She slipped quickly towards the door. “I'll tell uncle. You MUST see him for a minute or two.”

Secretly, Fred felt his future was protected against Mary's mocking predictions, quite apart from the “anything” he stood ready to do if she would only specify it. He never dared mention his expectations from Mr. Featherstone in her presence, and she always ignored them as though everything depended on Fred himself. But if he actually inherited the property, she would have to acknowledge his altered position. These thoughts passed rather sluggishly through him before he went upstairs. He stayed only briefly, pleading a cold. Mary did not return before he left. Riding home, however, he began to feel more aware of being ill than of being unhappy.

Caleb arrived at Stone Court shortly after dusk. Mary was not surprised, although he seldom had time to visit and disliked having to talk with Mr. Featherstone. The old man, in turn, felt uncomfortable with a brother-in-law he could not irritate, who did not mind being thought poor, wanted nothing from him, and understood every branch of farming and mining better than he did. Mary had been sure her parents would want to see her. If her father had not come, she would have asked leave to visit home for an hour or two the next day. After discussing prices over tea with Mr. Featherstone, Caleb rose to leave and said, “I need a word with you, Mary.”

She carried a candle into another large parlor where no fire was lit, set its weak light on the dark mahogany table, then turned and put her arms around his neck. She kissed him with the childish affection he delighted in. Beneath his broad brows his expression softened as a great, beautiful dog's does when petted. Mary was his favorite child. Whatever Susan said, and however right she was about everything else, Caleb thought it entirely natural that Fred or anyone should find Mary more lovable than other girls.
“I've something to tell you, my dear,” he began hesitantly. “Not very good news, though it could be worse.”
“About money, father? I think I know.”

“Do you? How could you? You see, I've been a bit foolish again and signed a bill, and now it must be paid. Your mother has to give up her savings. That's the worst part, and even they won't quite cover it. We need a hundred and ten pounds. She has ninety-two, and I've nothing to spare at the bank. She thinks you may have saved something.”
“Oh yes, more than twenty-four pounds. I thought you'd come, so I put it in my bag. Look! Lovely white notes and gold.”
Mary took the folded money from her small bag and placed it in his hand.

“But how—we need only eighteen. Here, put the rest back, child. How did you know?” Caleb asked. His incurable indifference to money was already giving way to a greater concern about what this might mean for Mary's affections.
“Fred told me this morning.”
“Ah. Did he come specially?”
“I think so. He was very upset.”

“I'm afraid Fred can't be trusted, Mary,” her father said with hesitant tenderness. “Perhaps he means better than he behaves. But I'd be sorry to see anyone's happiness tied to his, and so would your mother.”
“So would I, father,” Mary said without looking up, pressing the back of his hand against her cheek.

“I don't mean to pry, my dear. But I feared there might be something between you and Fred and wanted to warn you. You see, Mary”—his voice grew more tender; after pushing his hat about on the table and studying it, he finally looked at her—“however good a woman is, she must endure the life her husband makes for her. Your mother has endured a great deal because of me.”
Mary lifted the back of his hand to her lips and smiled at him.

“Well, nobody's perfect, but—” Mr. Garth shook his head to supply what words could not. “I'm thinking of what it must be like for a wife who can never rely on her husband, because there's no principle in him that makes him fear wronging others more than having his own toes trodden on. That's the whole of it, Mary. Young people may fall in love before they understand life and imagine it all a holiday if only they can be together. But it soon becomes a working day, my dear. Still, you have more sense than most and haven't been wrapped in cotton wool. Perhaps there's no need to tell you. But a father fears for his daughter, and you're alone here.”

“Don't worry about me,” Mary said, meeting his eyes seriously. “Fred has always been very kind to me. He's affectionate and good-hearted, and despite his self-indulgence I don't think he's false. But I'll never promise myself to a man without an adult's independence, who idles his time away hoping other people will support him. You and mother have taught me too much pride for that.”
“That's right. Quite right. Now I'm reassured,” said Mr. Garth, picking up his hat. “Still, it's hard to take away your earnings, isn't it, child?”
“Father!” Mary protested in her deepest voice. Her last words before he closed the outer door were, “Take pocketfuls of love home to everyone as well.”

“Your father wanted your wages, I suppose,” said old Mr. Featherstone when she returned, with his usual gift for unpleasant guesses. “He has a tight enough time, I reckon. You're of age now. You ought to save for yourself.”
“I consider my parents the best part of myself, sir,” Mary answered coldly.

Mr. Featherstone grunted. He could hardly deny that an ordinary girl like her might be expected to make herself useful, so he found another remark, unpleasant enough to suit any occasion. “If Fred Vincy comes tomorrow, don't keep him chatting. Send him up to me.”
